THE RULINGS (T-0839). Every cluster in merge_candidates.json is ruled here, in writing, and tools/merge_resident_cards.py --apply is what acts on them. MERGE is landed: the survivor takes the union and each folded card becomes a redirect stub at data/residents/merged/. DISTINCT and UNDECIDED are written onto the cards themselves, as `identity_rulings`, so the next pass does not re-ask. DEFERRED names the ticket that owns the pair.

ON `one source prints more than one of these cards`, which the candidate ledger files as evidence AGAINST nearly every cluster: read it carefully. `chicago_democrat_1833_1835` is a three-year run of a weekly, not a page, and the cards under it were minted from DIFFERENT issues months apart — that is a paper printing one man repeatedly, which is the normal case. The flag bites only where the two printings are the same line, or where the source is a LIST that names each person once: the 1833-1835 voter rolls, a census page, a directory. It is used that way in the Beaubien and Smith refusals and nowhere else.

ON THE GRADE: no ruling here grades anybody. A merged card is re-graded by the ladder — consolidate_resident_evidence.py --build then mint_civic_residents.py --regrade — never by taking the best of the folded grades, and each survivor carries `regrade_pending: true` until that has run.

rulings.why: THE DEMONSTRATION THE TICKET WAS OPENED ON. Four cards, one man: Lieut. James Allen, U.S. Army, the harbour engineer. `allen_lieut` and `allen_lieut_j` print the title and an initial; `allen_lieut_james` prints the title and the full name and is the only card that knows his trade (`army_officer`, the Democrat of 13 August 1834); `allen_james` is the card the ladder graded G1b on four sources and it knew nothing about the army. Nothing in the four contradicts anything in the others — no second forename, no second trade, no second seat — and every one of them is the Democrat, the American or the voter lists printing the same officer the way each set him. Merged he is one attested man with a trade and four sources; split he was four thin men. `allen_william` and `allen_edward_richards` are NOT in this cluster and are not touched: a title with no forename joins only a card carrying the same title.

THE SECOND DEMONSTRATION. Six cards for Gurdon Saltonstall Hubbard, the packer, whom Andreas, the American Fur Company's own record and the voter lists all name. `hubbard_g`, `hubbard_g_s`, `hubbard_g_t` and `hubbard_gurdon_s` are initials the papers set; `hubbard_gordon_s` is Gurdon spelled with an o, which is one letter at six and the printers' commonest error on this name. the cluster has an ANCHOR — one card carrying a documented identity from a biographical source (Andreas, a directory, a death notice) — and the rest are thin newspaper readings of the same name with no identity of their own. Where a thin card differs from the anchor only in a MIDDLE INITIAL, that letter is the least reliable thing in the corpus: it is one glyph in a newspaper column read through OCR, and the reading it produced is preserved whole in the stub. Where two thin cards contradict each other and NO anchor stands behind either, this pass does not pick one — see the UNDECIDED rulings. The one card that carries the identity — birth, trade, the fur company, the south division — is `hubbard_gurdon`, and it is the survivor. `hubbard_g_t`'s middle T is the weakest link in the cluster and it is folded rather than held: the town's records name no G. T. Hubbard and no second Gurdon, the reading stands whole in the stub, and Ahira, Elijah Kent, Henry G. and Otis Hubbard are not in this cluster at all.

Two men, not one. Both cards are ATTESTED at G1a with independent multi-source identities — William Smith on the Black Hawk enrolments, the 1840 census and both directories; William V. Smith on the Democrat and the voter lists — and the SAME 1833-1835 voter roll prints both, which is a roll naming each elector once. Smith is the commonest surname in the corpus and William the commonest forename; folding them on a bare initial would be the exact error name_agreement.py was written to stop.

held_apart.why: The 1833-1835 voter lists print William Smith and William V. Smith both, and each carries an independent multi-source identity. Two men.

rulings.why: A FATHER AND HIS SON, and they already stand on one card. Andreas names John Wright, merchant, and John S. Wright, clerk, his son — `hh_wright_john` carries both, the second with relationship `son`. Folding them would delete a person the sources explicitly count. `wright_j`, the American's bare `J Wright` of July 1835, could be either of them or a third Wright (Amasa, Robert C. and Truman G. also stand in the town), and no source reached decides it — that one is UNDECIDED and goes to the owner rather than to a guess.

held_apart.why: Andreas names John Wright the merchant and John S. Wright his son; the card already carries them as head and son.
Andreas names John S. Wright as the son of John Wright, and gives him his own trade (clerk). Not a duplicate of his father.

OWNER: the American of 11 July 1835 prints `J Wright` and nothing else. He is John Wright, or John S. Wright, or a fourth Wright the town already holds — Amasa, Robert C. and Truman G. stand on their own cards. No source reached decides it, and picking one would put a printing on a man on no evidence.

rulings.why: OWNER. Two thin readings and NO anchor: `John A Clark` is the Democrat of 11 February 1834 and `John K Clark` the American of 11 July 1835, each a single printing, neither carrying a trade, a seat or a biographical source. They agree on John and disagree on the middle letter. Where an anchor stands behind one card this pass folds the thin readings onto it; here there is nothing to fold onto, and picking one of two equal readings would invent the man it kept. Erastus and Timothy J. Clark are outside this cluster.

held_apart.why: Two single-printing readings, John A. and John K., with no biographical anchor behind either. Neither can be folded onto the other without inventing which one survives.

rulings.why: OWNER. `William S. Saunders` is a letter-list-only card; `William W Saunders` is a single Democrat printing of March 1834. Same paper, same forename, contradicted middle letter, no anchor behind either and no trade, seat or date to test. The town holds no third Saunders to break the tie.

held_apart.why: S against W in the middle initial, two thin readings, no biographical anchor behind either.

D. all stand on their own cards) and no anchor decides whether the bare reading is the same man. The owner's call.

held_apart.why: A bare `William Taylor` against `William H Taylor`, both thin Democrat readings, on a surname the town already carries five ways.

rulings.why: OWNER. `George E. Walker` is a letter-list card the Fergus 1843 death notices also reach; `George H Walker` is the Black Hawk enrolments and the Democrat at G1c. The middle letters contradict, both cards carry real independent evidence, and neither is anchored in a biographical source that would settle which letter the man used. James and Jeremiah Walker are outside this cluster.

held_apart.why: E against H in the middle initial, with independent evidence on both cards and no biographical anchor behind either.

rulings.why: TWO PEOPLE, not one card split — the opposite fault. `Mrs Rufus Brown` is a woman (sex female, relationship wife) whom the honorific strip folded onto her husband's forename, so the candidate pass sees `Rufus` on both. Andreas names the Green Tree tavern's keeper and his wife. They must not be merged. This pair is T-0723's — 'One identity, two town cards' — and that ticket is IN FLIGHT on another branch as this ruling is written. The reading is recorded here so the sweep is complete and no later pass re-asks; the CARDS are deliberately not touched, because two runs writing the same two records is how a merge queue loses work.

held_apart.why: Husband and wife, not one person: the honorific strip took `Mrs` off and left her carrying his forename. T-0723 owns the strip.
